setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. You are writing an email to tell a {client} that their {deliverable} will be late.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you are drafting a message to a {client} about a delay with their {deliverable}.
pressure: The {client} has asked about it three times today.
{coworker3} says to just send something quickly.
detail: The draft is about 150 words long.
You are writing it on the shared computer.

tiers.1: The facts in the message have to be right before anything else.
tiers.2: The reader has to be able to understand the words.
tiers.3: A calm, polite tone keeps the relationship intact.
tiers.4: The key information belongs at the start.
tiers.5: Proofreading is the last step once the content is right.

fact: You are not sure of the new date the {deliverable} will be ready.
clear: {Lead|the} confirmed that the new date is Thursday.
issues.done: the new date was already confirmed
issues.action: Confirm the new date with {lead|the} before putting it in the email.
issues.reason: A wrong date in writing creates a second broken promise. Confirming it first keeps the message accurate.
issues.lesson: Confirm the facts before you put them in writing.

shortcut.text: Write a date that seems likely and fix it later if needed.
shortcut.why: A guessed date in writing is a promise you may not keep.
shortcut.mis: Written dates can be changed easily later.

fact: Your draft uses the team's shorthand codes, which the {client} will not know.
issues.action: Replace the shorthand with plain words the {client} will understand.
issues.reason: The {client} cannot act on a message they cannot understand.
issues.lesson: Write in words your reader knows.

shortcut.text: Keep the codes, since they are more precise.
shortcut.why: Precision does not help if the reader cannot decode it.

fact: Your draft sounds irritated, because the {client} has asked about the order three times.
issues.action: Revise the draft so it sounds calm and polite.
issues.brief: make the tone calm and polite
issues.reason: The {client}'s questions are reasonable. An irritated tone damages the relationship.
issues.lesson: Match your tone to a respectful professional relationship.

shortcut.text: Keep the tone, since the {client} needs to stop asking.
shortcut.why: An irritated tone may make the {client} more upset, not less.
shortcut.mis: Showing frustration makes people stop asking.

fact: The ready date and what happens next are buried in the fourth paragraph.
issues.action: Move the new date and next step into the first two sentences.
issues.brief: move the key facts to the top
issues.reason: Readers look for the key facts first. Putting them up front makes the message clear at a glance.
issues.lesson: Put the most important information first.

shortcut.text: Leave it, since the {client} will read the whole thing.
shortcut.why: Many readers skim. Buried facts get missed.

fact: You have not proofread the draft yet.
issues.action: Proofread the email for spelling and grammar before you send it.
issues.reason: Errors distract the reader and make the message look careless.
issues.lesson: Proofread before sending anything a customer will read.

shortcut.text: Send it now and correct any errors in a follow-up.
shortcut.why: A follow-up correction draws more attention to the mistakes.
shortcut.mis: Errors do not matter if you fix them later.

clear: You already proofread the draft twice.

proceed.why: The message is accurate, clear and polite, so it is ready to send.
proceed.lesson: Send a message once it is accurate, clear and suited to the reader.

generic.text: Call the {client} and say you will email something eventually.
generic.why: A vague promise adds nothing. The {client} needs the actual information.
generic.mis: Contacting someone is the same as informing them.

generic.text: Ask {coworker2} to write and send it under your name.
generic.why: Someone else writing under your name is misleading and avoids your job.
generic.mis: It does not matter who writes a message.

overcaution.text: Ask {lead|the} to rewrite the whole email before you send it.
overcaution.why: The email is ready. A full rewrite delays the {client}'s answer.

title: Draft: update on your {deliverable}
intro: Check this draft before it goes to the {client}.
prompt: Which line needs to be fixed before sending?
doc.lesson: Clear customer emails lead with the facts, use plain words, keep a polite tone and follow writing conventions.

lines.text: Your {deliverable} will be ready Thursday, two days later than planned.
A part we needed arrived late from our supplier.

bad.text: The delay is due to a BO on SKU 44-B per the PO.
bad.why: Abbreviations the {client} does not know make the reason unclear.

lines.text: We are sorry for the inconvenience.

bad.text: As we have told you several times, these things take time.
bad.why: The tone is irritated and talks down to the {client}.

lines.text: We will call you Thursday morning when it is ready.
Please let us know if you have any questions.

bad.text: please let us no if you has any questions
bad.why: Spelling, grammar and capitalization errors make the message look careless.

bad.text: Your {deliverable} should be ready by Monday at the latest.
bad.why: This contradicts the opening line, which says Thursday. Conflicting dates confuse the reader.

setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. You are about to follow a written procedure for {task|the} for the first time.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you have been handed a written procedure for {task|the}.
pressure: {coworker3} says nobody actually reads the whole procedure.
{Lead|the} wants the task done before lunch.
detail: The procedure is three pages long.
It is printed on colored paper.

tiers.1: When two documents disagree, find out which one is current first.
tiers.2: A warning section has to be read in full before you start.
tiers.3: An unknown term can change what a step means.
tiers.4: The revision date tells you whether the copy is current.

fact: The printed procedure and the copy posted on the wall give different steps for the same part.
issues.action: Ask {lead|the} which version is current before you continue.
issues.reason: Following the wrong version could mean doing the task incorrectly. The lead knows which one is current.
issues.lesson: When documents conflict, find out which is current before acting.

shortcut.why: Easier is not the same as current or correct.
shortcut.mis: The simplest instructions are the right ones.

fact: You skimmed the procedure and skipped a boxed section labeled "Caution."
issues.action: Go back and read the caution section in full before starting.
issues.reason: Caution sections hold the information most likely to prevent mistakes or injuries.
issues.lesson: Read warnings and cautions in full before starting a task.

shortcut.text: Start the task and read the caution if something goes wrong.
shortcut.brief: read it only if something goes wrong
shortcut.why: The caution is meant to prevent problems, not explain them afterward.
shortcut.mis: Warnings are only needed when trouble starts.

fact: Step 4 uses a term you do not know.
clear: The glossary on the last page explains the term.
issues.done: the glossary already explains the term
issues.action: Check the glossary or ask {coworker} what the term means.
issues.brief: find out what the term means
issues.reason: Guessing at a term can change what the step means.
issues.lesson: Clarify words you do not know before acting on instructions.

shortcut.text: Guess what it means from the rest of the sentence.
shortcut.why: A wrong guess can mean doing the step incorrectly.
shortcut.mis: Context always makes a term's meaning clear.

fact: The procedure has a revision date from three years ago.
clear: The revision date shows it was updated last month.
issues.done: the procedure is already confirmed as current
issues.action: Ask {lead|the} whether a newer version of the procedure exists.
issues.brief: ask if there is a newer version
issues.reason: Procedures change. An old copy may be missing current steps.
issues.lesson: Check that a document is current before relying on it.

shortcut.text: Follow it as written, since procedures rarely change.
shortcut.why: Three years is a long time. Steps may have changed.
shortcut.mis: Old documents are as reliable as new ones.

proceed.text: Follow the procedure step by step.
proceed.why: The procedure is current, clear and complete, so following it carefully is the right move.
proceed.lesson: When a procedure is current and understood, follow it step by step.

generic.text: Ask {coworker2} to just show you instead of reading anything.
generic.why: Watching once may miss steps the written procedure covers.
generic.mis: Watching is always better than reading.

generic.text: Skip to the last page to see what the end result looks like and go from there.
generic.why: Skipping the steps risks missing what each one requires.
generic.mis: Knowing the result is enough to do a task.

overcaution.text: Ask {lead|the} to read the whole procedure aloud to you first.
overcaution.why: The procedure is clear and current. Having it read aloud wastes the lead's time.
overcaution.mis: Instructions are only safe if a supervisor reads them out.

title: Procedure: {task}
intro: You are checking this procedure before it is reprinted.
prompt: Which line is unclear or wrong?
doc.lesson: Clear procedures use exact wording, keep steps in order and agree with themselves.

lines.text: Revised: this month. Replaces all earlier versions.
Step 1: Gather the items listed on the checklist.
Step 2: Check each item against the checklist before starting.

bad.text: Step 2: Do the usual checks, more or less.
bad.why: "The usual checks, more or less" is too vague to follow.

lines.text: Step 3: Record the start time in {record|the}.

bad.text: Step 3: Write down the time somewhere.
bad.why: "Somewhere" is vague; the procedure should name where to record it.

lines.text: Step 4: Complete the task, then record the finish time.

bad.text: Step 4: Record the finish time, then complete the task.
bad.why: You cannot record a finish time before the task is finished.

lines.text: Step 5: Return all items to their places.

bad.text: Note: for Step 3, keep using last year's version of this procedure.
bad.why: The top line says this revision replaces all earlier versions, so pointing to last year's version contradicts it.

review.notes: Interpreting documents. Conflicting copies and an old revision date overlap, so they are exclusive.
